title: DOES GOD EXPECT YOU TO BE PERFECT?
paragraphs:
DOES GOD EXPECT YOU TO BE PERFECT?
The Verse That Has Terrified Christians—and the Grace We Keep Missing
And depending on what you believe God means by them, they can either pull you toward your Father...
or make you terrified to come near Him.
Maybe nobody knows how exhausted you are from trying to be the Christian you think God expects.
You pray, but sometimes your mind wanders.
You worship, but Monday arrives and anxiety comes back.
You promised God you would never return to that sin... and then you returned.
You told yourself you had forgiven them, until their name appeared on your screen and something ugly rose inside your chest.
You know how to smile when someone at church asks, “How are you?”
But there are nights when the performance ends.
And the question you would never say in front of everybody else crawls out of the darkness:
God... how disappointed are You in me?
Because Jesus really did say something frighteningly serious:
“Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect.” — Matthew 5:48
And if we rip that sentence away from everything surrounding it, we can turn Christianity into an impossible treadmill:
But what if the command of Jesus is far deeper—and far more beautiful—than the perfectionism that has been strangling you?
“Ἔσεσθε οὖν ὑμεῖς τέλειοι ὡς ὁ πατὴρ ὑμῶν ὁ οὐράνιος τέλειός ἐστιν.”
The word translated “perfect” is τέλειοι — teleioi, from τέλειος — teleios.
It can carry the sense of being complete, mature, brought toward its intended goal.
That does not mean Jesus is saying sin does not matter.
It does not mean holiness is optional.
And it certainly does not mean, “Relax. God doesn't care how you live.”
Jesus never lowered God's holiness to make sinners comfortable.
He came to save sinners who could never reach God's holiness by themselves.
And the context of Matthew 5:48 matters enormously.
Immediately before this statement, Jesus says:
“Do good to them that hate you.”
“Pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you.”
Then Jesus points toward the Father, who sends sunlight and rain without limiting His common kindness only to people we think deserve it.
“Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect.”
Jesus is not handing His disciples a checklist for neurotic religious flawlessness.
He is calling them into a mature, whole, Father-reflecting love that refuses to love only the lovable.
And suddenly the verse becomes even more confronting.
Because some of us would rather be religiously impressive than love our enemies.
We would rather count how many chapters we read than forgive the person who wounded us.
We would rather post a Bible verse than pray sincerely for someone who betrayed us.
We would rather appear holy than allow Jesus to invade the bitter room in our hearts where we have kept someone's name locked away for years.
But biblical holiness is not cosmetic Christianity.
The pride nobody corrects because we learned to disguise it as spiritual confidence.
The resentment we justify because “they deserve it.”
The addiction we keep renaming a struggle because repentance sounds too final.
The private compromise beneath the public worship.
And this is where perfectionism becomes dangerous.
Come into the light because you cannot heal yourself.
Make yourself acceptable, then approach God.
Christ came precisely because sinners could never make themselves acceptable before a holy God.
Perfectionism makes failure the end of your story.
Jesus makes repentance the doorway into another chapter.
This distinction matters because Scripture refuses to pretend Christians instantly become incapable of sin.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:8–9
Notice what Christianity does not say.
It does not say sin is imaginary.
It does not say guilt is always unhealthy.
It does not say repentance is unnecessary.
It says something far more powerful:
Your sin is real, but the blood of Jesus is greater.
There is a difference between conviction and condemnation.
Conviction drags the hidden wound into the light so Christ can deal with it.
Condemnation tells you there is no point coming home.
Condemnation says, “You might as well die with it.”
Condemnation tries to turn your sin into your identity.
But the Gospel announces that for the one who belongs to Jesus Christ:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 8:1
Not because your sin became harmless.
That is why the cross is so offensive to human pride.
We desperately want to contribute something to our rescue.
Surely being better than that person counts.
But stand beneath the cross long enough and every spiritual résumé begins falling apart.
You don't see Jesus dying beside your accomplishments.
You see Jesus dying in the place of sinners.
The nails announce something your pride hates admitting:
But those same nails announce something your shame desperately needs to hear:
Jesus did not wait for you to become worth saving before He came to save you.
“For when we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly.” — Romans 5:6
Grace did not arrive after the cleanup.
This is why Christianity is not the story of good people becoming slightly better.
It is the story of spiritually dead sinners receiving life through Jesus Christ.
It is guilty people being justified.
And perhaps the most astonishing tension appears in Hebrews.
“μιᾷ γὰρ προσφορᾷ τετελείωκεν εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς τοὺς ἁγιαζομένους.”
“For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.”
And His people are still being sanctified.
You are not accepted because you finally became impressive enough for God.
Those who are in Christ stand on Christ's finished work.
And the same grace that saves does not leave us comfortably chained to the sins from which Jesus came to deliver us.
Grace welcomes the filthy prodigal home.
And grace does not tell him to move the pigpen into the Father's house.
Maybe that is the sentence somebody needs tonight.
Because there are two lies destroying people in opposite directions.
“I keep failing, therefore God could never want me.”
“God forgives me, therefore I don't need to change.”
Grace is free to us because its cost was paid by Christ.
And the grace that pardons us begins reshaping us.
“Οὐχ ὅτι ἤδη ἔλαβον ἢ ἤδη τετελείωμαι...”
“Not that I have already obtained, or am already made perfect...”
And he refuses to pretend he has reached final perfection.
But he does not use imperfection as permission to stop pursuing Christ.
That may be the word you needed.
You discovered pride in yourself again?
Your prayer life has become cold?
You've been secretly fighting something you are ashamed to name?
Cut off what feeds the sin.
Christian maturity is not pretending you never stumble.
It is becoming increasingly unwilling to make peace with what nailed your Savior to a cross.
There is a massive difference between struggling against sin and settling into sin.
But the Spirit keeps calling us toward Christ.
Imagine remembering every boast you made about your loyalty.
Peter had every reason to believe his greatest failure would become the title over the rest of his life.
But Jesus was not finished writing Peter's story.
After the resurrection, beside a charcoal fire, Jesus restored the disciple who had denied Him.
Three denials did not get the final word.
And Jesus entrusted work to a man with scars in his testimony.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Not editing the ugly chapters out of your biography.
But discovering that when Jesus becomes Lord of the story, even the chapter you thought destroyed everything can become the place where grace shines brightest.
Maybe your scandal never became public.
Maybe only you and God know.
Maybe it happened years ago and you still punish yourself every morning for something Christ is calling you to bring fully beneath His mercy.
Maybe your “scandal” isn't sexual sin or addiction.
A lie that grew larger than you intended.
Maybe you're reading this while carrying the terrifying thought:
If people knew everything about me, they would never look at me the same way again.
And the Gospel invitation is not:
Confession is when you stop defending what He came to forgive and transform.
Repentance is not purchasing forgiveness with enough tears.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior.
Faith is not confidence in your ability to maintain a flawless record.
It is resting your hope in Jesus Christ—crucified and risen—and entrusting yourself to Him.
Does God expect you to be perfect?
If by “perfect” you mean, “Does God demand holiness, wholehearted allegiance, mature love, and transformation toward Christlikeness?”
Jesus does not call us to comfortable compromise.
“Be ye holy; for I am holy.” — 1 Peter 1:16
But if by “perfect” you mean, “Must I achieve sinless personal perfection through my own performance before God will receive me?”
That is precisely why you need a Savior.
If you could produce the righteousness necessary to rescue yourself, Calvary would be unnecessary.
The Gospel is not God lowering His standard until you can jump over it.
The Gospel is Jesus fulfilling what you could not, bearing sin at the cross, rising from the dead, and becoming the hope of everyone who turns to Him in repentant faith.
The person who used to enjoy sin begins grieving it.
The person who never forgave begins learning forgiveness.
The person enslaved to approval begins discovering identity in Christ.
The sexually broken begin learning purity.
Because Christianity is not behavior modification with Jesus stickers attached.
And maybe this explains why you're so tired.
You have been trying to produce with willpower what can only grow through abiding in Christ.
“Without me ye can do nothing.” — John 15:5
You need Him when you fail.
You need Him when you succeed.
You need Him when temptation screams.
You need Him when worship feels effortless.
You need Him when the Bible seems alive.
You need Him when you read three paragraphs and feel nothing.
You need Jesus on your best Christian day every bit as truly as on your worst.
Because Jesus isn't merely the emergency room you visit after sin.
More willing to obey when obedience costs something?
More willing to love someone who cannot repay me?
More captivated by Christ than I was before?
That is a much harder mirror.
But it is also a far healthier one.
Because maturity does not make you increasingly impressed with yourself.
The closer you walk with Jesus, the less attractive self-glory becomes.
Every step toward holiness is evidence that God has not abandoned His work.
And when you stumble, you stop running away from the only One who can restore you.
Maybe you've spent years hiding because you believed God was waiting for the perfected version of you.
There is no perfected version of you waiting somewhere outside Christ.
There is only the sinner you are...
and the Savior who calls you.
Come with the sin you're finally ready to stop defending.
He is not asking you to become your own savior.
He is commanding you to follow the Savior you desperately need.
And if you've experienced the patience of Christ while He continues changing you, tell somebody beneath this article:
Your comment may become the sentence another struggling believer needed to discover they are not the only Christian fighting a battle behind a smile.
And think of one person who desperately needs this truth.
The friend who thinks God has given up on them.
The son who stopped attending church because shame became unbearable.
The daughter silently questioning whether she can ever come home.
The believer trapped between addiction and self-hatred.
The religious person who looks spotless publicly but is collapsing privately.
Send this directly to them if the conversation needs to remain private.
We glorify God through faith in Christ and lives of loving obedience.

And if this ministry is helping you follow Jesus, stay close. Invite your family. Invite your friends. Invite struggling believers. Invite seekers. Invite the lukewarm. Even invite the unbeliever who has questions nobody has taken seriously.
But before you leave, remember the question that brought you here:
Does God expect you to be perfect?
He calls you toward the perfection, maturity, holiness, and wholehearted love revealed in Christ.
But He never told you to save yourself.
The Christian life is not a flawless person presenting God with an impressive record.
It is a redeemed sinner clinging to a flawless Savior while the Holy Spirit continues the transforming work of sanctification.
Don't make peace with the sin.
Because your worst chapter does not have authority to write the ending.
The hands that were pierced for your sin are still holding the pen.
